https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: The UK's seasons are changing, with fewer winter frosts and more hot summer days, according to new analysis from the Met Office.
Across the UK, the number of winter days with an air frost – when the air temperature falls to 0C or below – was around a quarter lower in the decade to 2025 than during the period from 1961 to 1990.
In southern England, the reduction was around a third while the average number of UK summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled.
The Met Office says climate change has led to these seasonal shifts.
"Our summer is getting wider and our winter is getting smaller," says Dr James Pope, climate scientist at the Met Office.
"The driver of this is that the whole global climate is warming. And that impacts on the UK.
"Some areas went from their wettest ever winter to a severe drought via a record-breaking summer for the whole country."
The changing conditions have affected wildlife and led some farmers to grow different crops.
Some of the biggest reductions in winter air frosts have been in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, where the average number of days has fallen by around 11 compared with 1961 to 1990.
Southern England has seen other significant changes. In Cornwall, the average number of winter air frost days has almost halved, falling from around 18 to just 10.
On the Isle of Wight, the figure has also fallen by almost half, from around 21 to 11 days.
Scotland remains the frostiest UK nation, but has also seen a reduction, from around 45 to 38 winter air frost days.
Summer days reaching 25C have become more common across the UK.
Some of the biggest increases have been in southern England, where the average number of summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled, from just over eight to more than 16.
In Essex and Suffolk, they have risen by almost 13 days in both counties.
The Met Office defines a hot day as one where the temperature reaches 30C or above.
Across the UK, the average number of these days has increased fourfold, from 0.3 to 1.2 per summer.
The increase is particularly striking in Greater London, where days reaching 30C have risen from an average of 1.3 to 6.1 per summer.
Summer 2026 was the hottest on record , according to provisional Met Office data.
There were five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C, smashing the previous record of 34 days.
Tim Young's onions have been smaller than usual making them harder to sell to supermarkets

"Humans, animals and crops are encountering extremes of temperature that we've not seen before and this is a physiological challenge to all three," says Thomas Crocker, science manager with the Met Office's climate security team.
This has led to water challenges, he says, with wet winters causing problems with planting, pests and diseases.
Dry summers have meant there has not been enough water to grow crops.
"The impact on horticulture is seismic, it's affected all crops," says John Walgate, CEO of British Growers, which represents most British horticultural organisations growing vegetable and fruit.
Walgate says this year's weather has been particularly tough for brassicas like cauliflowers, cabbages and broccoli, with yields down by about 50%.
Irrigated crops such as onions, potatoes and carrots also suffered from a lack of water due to low rainfall and hot temperatures.
It's not all been bad though. Walgate says soft fruit such as strawberries have had a "good year".
Tim Young and his family have been farming in Norfolk since the 1960s.
But his arable crops - onions, wheat and sugar beet - have been struggling because of the hotter, drier summers and fewer cold days in winter which kill bugs.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8d: The asteroid before (left) and after, showing the crater left behind by a spacecraft's impact
The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.

The extensive damage was caused when a Nasa spacecraft hit the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. The asteroid posed no threat, but this was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.
Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.
"The crater is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular," said Dr Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist, who is on the Hera science team.
"It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to actually finally see what happened. And as a crater person, I can also say it's beautiful."
The original 2022 crash test was carried out by a Nasa spacecraft called Dart which hurtled into Dimorphos at 14,000mph (22,000km/h).
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 6,200 miles long (10,000km), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

Dimorphos is about 150m (500ft) wide and was partly chosen as the target because it is one of an asteroid pair - it orbits around a larger space rock called Didymos, which is about 730m (2,400ft) wide.
The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.
Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.
Watch: Moment Nasa spacecraft leaves stadium-sized crater in asteroid
A key objective of the Hera mission is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, in order to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.
This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.
"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.
"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."
Hera's arrival on the scene is helping scientists answer many more questions too.
Not only did the collision alter the shape of Dimorphos, it also changed the way it moves.
"Before the Dart impact, Dimorphos was more like our own Moon - so it was always showing the same face to Didymos, and it was behaving quite nicely," explained Raducan.

"Now it's very, very chaotic - it's tumbling. Imagine a barrel that you throw down the stairs, and the barrel is rolling and it's moving, and basically that's what Dimorphos does right now around Didymos."
Hera has also taken detailed images of Didymos, revealing its surface in detail.
"The gravity at the surface of Didymos is about 40,000 times less than the gravity on Earth," said Naomi Murdoch, who is on the Hera mission team.
"We can already see some fascinating and complex geology. We can see regions of boulders.

"The smallest details that we can make out in these images are about 3m in size. So that means that all the boulders that you can see with your eyes are at least 3m big, and some as big as 10m. So what we're seeing here is boulders the size of cars and buses sitting on a world with almost no gravity."
The mission has sent back new pictures of the smaller Dimorphos orbiting around Didymos
The Hera mission will spend the next six months studying Dimorphos and Didymos, sending back more images taken from closer up in higher resolution.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2: A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: The sun shone on 2025's Thanksgiving Parade but the forecast this year is not so bright
Strong winds are threatening to disrupt Thursday's Thanksgiving parade in New York City for the first time since World War Two.

A potent Nor'easter storm could impact the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade which is due to be taking place for the 100th time, with the risk that it could be too windy for the event's iconic balloons to fly.

The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade is due to end.
Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern USA as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow.
Western areas of the country have also faced Thanksgiving travel headaches, with Pacific storms and coastal flooding.
Storms targeting both US coasts threaten to snarl Thanksgiving travel for millions
The parade started life as the Macy's Christmas Parade, organised by employees at Macy's department store in New York City in a bid to boost holiday sales.
The first event took place on Thanksgiving Day 1924. It has only been cancelled during World War Two, when it was put on hiatus between 1942 and 1944. As a result, this year marks the 100th parade.

It is due to take place from 08:30 local time (13:30 GMT), ending at around 12:00 (17:00 GMT) , and involves marching bands, street performers and floats parading through the streets of New York City, as well as 100 brightly-coloured inflatable balloons.
Confetti filled the air above this enormous turkey at the start of the 2025 parade
However, due to city regulations full-size balloons cannot fly if sustained winds exceed 23mph (37km/h), or in gusts of more than 35mph (56km/h).
There is a risk that Thursday will bring winds approaching those strengths.
However, record wind gusts also made the 1997 route a no-fly zone and the balloons were still featured in the parade.
The giant character balloons were tethered to golf carts that year.
In 1989, when a major snowstorm stopped balloon handlers getting to the parade route, the cheer and dance teams stepped in to pull the giant balloons along.
Over the last few days, a cluster of showers and thunderstorms has been swarming in the Gulf of Mexico.

That area of disturbed weather is now moving northwards, close to the east coast, and deepening into a potent area of low pressure - a Nor'easter storm, so called because it delivers strong north-easterly winds which drive into the east coast.
The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning for New York City, as well as Long Island and north-east New Jersey.
It comes into force part-way through the parade and warns of strong to damaging wind gusts, which could affect trees and power lines and bring significant travel disruption.

The winds are forecast to strengthen through the day peaking during the evening, meaning the very strongest gusts are likely to hit after the parade is over. However, there is a risk that they could approach the threshold that would ground the balloons.
Up to 3in (75mm) of rain could fall with the risk of flooding, which could be exacerbated along the coast as high tides arrive on Thursday evening.
Large waves and high sea levels are expected, bringing the threat of erosion and damage along the shoreline.
Other eastern parts of the USA will also receive heavy rain and strong winds, with snow in some inland parts adding to the Thanksgiving travel headaches.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x2: Historic space mission lifts off with first Pakistani astronaut aboard Chinese rocket

China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.
Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.
Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".
The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".
While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the effects of space on living organisms.
The mission comprises of payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, flight engineer Wu Yi and commander Tang Hongbo
They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.
Ali will conduct studies on photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of radiation and microgravity - a very weak gravity in space - on seeds.
The former fighter pilot will return to Earth after a short stay, with two other Chinese crew members who have been at the space station since May.

Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, which lifted off in May this year. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.
China has poured billions of dollars into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
It is now keen to show the world that the station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.
Hundreds of people gathered at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center before dawn waving Chinese and Pakistani flags.

This also comes at a time when Beijing is trying to establish itself as a major alternative to the US-led space programme, with a bold goal to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030.
For Pakistan, which does not have its own spacecraft to send astronauts to space, being invited to be a part of this mission is significant.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: Christmas Day is a month away and as the festive season approaches you may start to wonder - could 2026 be a 'white Christmas'?
Over the past 65 years, there have been 41 white Christmases, meaning we are more likely than not to see one somewhere in the UK.
Forecasting the chances of a month ahead of the big day is a bit like staring into a crystal ball - but are there any early omens of snow on the festive horizon?

For a Christmas to be officially declared as 'white', a single snowflake needs to be recorded falling at any point during 25 December, at any of the Met Office's network of around 300 weather stations.
It means there doesn't have to be a thick covering of snow on the ground to qualify.
Indeed, the landscape could be beautifully festive and white with lying snow, but if no new snow falls on Christmas Day it cannot technically be called a white Christmas.
The last widespread white Christmas was in 2010, when snow fell at 19% of measuring stations and a significant 83% of stations reported snow lying on the ground.
Every year from 2020 to 2023 was officially a white Christmas, however very few places actually reported settling snow.
In December 2010 the UK experienced low temperatures and significant snowfalls. Lying snow was reported in many places on Christmas Day
A number of factors will influence the UK's weather in the run-up to the festive season.
A major one is the record-breaking El Niño which is, scientists predict, approaching its peak in the Pacific.

El Niño's strongest impacts tend to be felt close to where the phenomenon occurs, in the tropical Pacific, but the energy it releases into the atmosphere can send ripples through weather patterns across the globe.

Strong El Niño events can increase the odds of wet and stormy weather during the late autumn and early winter, and some studies suggest they can raise the chances of colder weather later in the season - but the evidence from past El Niños is decidedly mixed.
Will El Niño and the polar vortex bring snow to the UK this winter?
Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El Niño affect the UK weather?
Earlier in November the winds of the stratospheric polar vortex weakened and reversed, marking the earliest sudden stratospheric warming event on record.
This phenomenon tends to occur much later in winter and can - but doesn't always - weaken the jet stream, increasing the chance of cold northerly or easterly winds.
Occurring so early in the season, the effects this time are harder to quantify. It is not known what - if any - impact it will have on the weather over the weeks ahead.

The latest predictions from scientists at the Met Office , external , taking these and other factors into account, suggest there could be an increased likelihood of colder and drier-than-average conditions during the winter months of December, January and February.

However this only represents an increased probability of these conditions and - even if this occurs across the season as a whole - there are still very likely to be shorter-term periods of milder, wetter weather.
It is often tricky to accurately forecast snow in the UK, even a day or two in advance.
Snow requires just the right combination of cold air and moisture, and small changes in either of these elements can mean predicted snow actually falls as rain or vice versa.
It goes without saying that longer range snow forecasts are even more challenging and with Christmas still a month away it is impossible to offer precise predictions.
You can keep up to date with the latest forecast by checking BBC Weather online and the app .

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy0: As food inflation rises, vegetables are becoming an increasingly expensive part of the household budget
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data , external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall , external , India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Onion prices have surged, adding to the pressure on household food budgets
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.

"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.

Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis , external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.

Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.

And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c680: Paul Whitehouse unveiled the ice sculpture outside the prime minister's office in Manchester
Comedian and TV presenter Paul Whitehouse has called for the government to help save an at-risk fish species present in England's largest lake since the end of the last Ice Age.

Windermere, in the Lake District, has been home to Arctic charr for more than 10,000 years, but campaigners warn extinction beckons as the fish's habitat is harmed by sewage pollution, invasive species competing for food and rising temperatures caused by global warming.
Whitehouse urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to act and said it would be "a crime" if the species were lost.
The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it shared "the public's determination to protect this iconic lake".

Whitehouse, who fronts the BBC's Mortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Fishing series alongside fellow comedian Bob Mortimer, said the "spawning grounds for this beautiful species are covered in algal sludge that is a direct result of sewage pollution".
Arctic charr have been described as a "living link to the end of the last Ice Age"

The former Fast Show star is helping environmental campaigner Matt Staniek unveil a 1.3m (5ft 6in) ice sculpture depicting the prime minister outside No 10 North, in Manchester, to highlight the fish's plight.
Staniek wants the prime minister to expedite a £3.7bn scheme that would include a huge tunnel carrying sewage to a new state-of-the-art water treatment works .

It has been drawn up by the Only Rainwater In Windermere coalition comprising United Utilities (UU), the Environment Agency, Lake District National Park Authority (LDNPA), the Love Windermere partnership, Save Windermere campaign group and Westmorland and Furness Council.
It comes as new research from the Freshwater Biological Association (FBA) also warns Arctic charr are in serious decline and face extinction in the lake without "urgent action".

The fish, which is genetically distinct from Arctic charr in the region's other lakes, lives in four separate populations in Windermere that spawn at different times of year and different places and do not interbreed.

The FBA said spawning habitat quality had "declined markedly" at Windermere since 2017 with levels of silt and algae increasing while introduced species, such as ruffe, roach and bream, were "on the rise".
Windermere has long been popular with visitors but it faces a number of pressures, campaigners say
Dr Louise Lavictoire, the organisation's head of science, said the research had "shown very clearly that we are at risk of losing Arctic charr from Windermere completely".
"The species is facing multiple pressures and research gives us the evidence, data and sense of urgency to take collective action to protect this ancient fish species before it's too late."
The research was funded by groups including Natural England, the Environment Agency and the LDNPA.
Natural England's Dave Ottewell described Arctic charr as "remarkable fish" and a "living link to the end of the last Ice Age".
Tim Duckmanton, team leader for strategy and environment at the LDNPA, echoed that sentiment and said "thanks to data collected, we now have a better understanding of threats to the species".

UU, which manages infrastructure around the lake, said protecting the area was a "priority" and that £200m was being invested over the next four years in an effort to cut spills from storm overflows and improve wastewater treatment.

A Defra spokesperson said: "This government is already acting to reduce sewage discharges, including deploying 33 additional Environment Agency specialists in the region, increasing inspections and through our regional water council's giving the local community in Windermere a greater say in decision making.

If you're shopping Black Friday or Cyber Monday sales , don't rely on AI to get you the best prices.
Ecommerce agency Keetrax this week asked five AI assistants for Black Friday deals in the way a shopper would, and then checked the deals quoted against the shops' websites.

Three different AIs sent shoppers to Briscoes for air fryer deals Briscoes wasn't offering. Google AI Mode quoted a Brabantia at $79; on Briscoes' site it was $299.99. Gemini had a Zip at $99, an offer that had ended, when the real price was $379.99. Claude had a Russell Hobbs at $160 that was $399.99.

Google AI Mode matched seven of its 12 deals, the fewest of the five: four were wrong and one couldn't be checked. It had the biggest miss of the check when it said a barbecue at Heathcotes, a family-owned Waikato retailer, was "sitting at the higher end around $4299" when Heathcotes was selling it for $1047.
In six cases the shop was cheaper than the AI said, so a retailer with a real deal was missing out on the sale .

Managing director Danielle Martel said the AI seemed to be relying on incorrect data. "There are a lot of sales going on and we're in peak sales season so the prices are changing quite a bit. The algorithm is probably picking up on old pricing that's happened in the past, it's not updating fast enough or it could be hallucinating."

She said the concern was that shoppers were getting "lazier and lazier". "I think they do rely on it and I wouldn't put it past them to go into a shop and try to purchase that Briscoes air fryer for $79 when it's actually $299.

"I think AI is really good for trying to find out the features, the benefits and maybe doing a little bit of background research on terms of whether they can get it local or there's a better price somewhere else, but they do need to actually click on to the merchant's website and check the prices."

"This year's the worst year for businesses going out of business and I think if a business that might be getting overlooked that has a better price than some of the bigger merchants in New Zealand or businesses owned and operated offshore, then yeah, we are missing out, we are losing money in our economy and we're not supporting maybe the smaller merchants that are around."
She said AI also seemed to favour large retailers over independent shops.

University of Auckland commercial law lecturer Alex Sims, a technology expert for Nine to Noon , said it could be a case of out of date information being picked up but was also simply AI not being reliable.

"And on this report it's not just the occasional mistake. Serves as a warning for people not to blindly rely on AI. And that they need to be very careful using AI to purchase products for them as they could get a nasty surprise."
Chirs Wilkinson, of First Retail Group, said he had heard from retailers whose customers had come in with AI research and found the prices were not what they expected.

"I have heard about a number of these cases in the past few days, but you can expect that the issue is likely more widespread. People love the 'enablement' of AI, but as we know, it too needs challenging and it is only as good as the commands you provide.

Warning: This story contains details of assisted dying and may be upsetting for some readers.
New research has found a number of barriers are making it difficult those wanting to access assisted dying .

A new study showed low awareness from the public, confusion over eligibility, difficulty contacting the services, and practitioners not referring patients were all barriers for those seeking an assisted death .
The study interviewed 46 people who had sought assisted dying, as well as their family members.
Author and Victoria University senior research fellow Jessica Young said there were compounding factors to like access to technology making the situation worse.
The service worked by putting a request through a call-centre that then went to an assisted dying service. A clinical advisor would then call the person requesting assisted dying back, she said.
What worked against that, Young said, was a prohibition on health practitioners raising assisted dying.
"This has been interpreted to say that those clinical advisors can't say why they're calling," she said.
"It's this ambiguous phone call that you receive from Health NZ, which can be easily confused with Healthcare NZ which delivers home care."
Young said one man in the study had done exactly that, turning down the assisted dying service thinking it was home care.
Young said there were almost 1300 applications for assisted dying in the latest reporting year, with close to 500 people having an assisted death.
Three hundred and six people died waiting for an assisted death.
Young said the system worked well most of the time, but the hurdles still existed.
"People have really limited time at the end of life, and also really limited energy," she said.
"That tenacity that's required to navigate these barriers, and to over come them is something that we would like to see changed."
One of the things that would help with that would be to provide information in the healthcare setting, Young said.
She said there was an argument for a public education campaign around assisted death.
"Most people who access assisted dying are already having palliative care, but people may not know what palliative care is or how they access that as well," Young said.
"There's definitely greater public education in raising the health literacy and death literacy of New Zealanders."
The End of Life Choice Act started as a private member's bill introduced by ACT leader David Seymour in 2017.
It became law in 2021 after passing a conscience vote in Parliament and gaining roughly two-to-one support in a referendum held alongside the 2020 general election.
The ACT Party has a private members bill before Parliament that could ease the restrictions on assisted dying , by removing the requirements for a terminal illness and a six-month prognosis.

However, opponents of a law change fear disabled people could then opt for assisted dying - not because they wanted it, but because they felt they were a burden on their families or were unable to get the support, housing and care they needed, especially in an era of cuts to health and disability services.
If it is an emergency and you feel like you or someone else is at risk, call 111.

One of the best investments of the past decade is also one that people should be wary about putting all their money into, market commentators say.
Over the past ten years, Bitcoin has had the strongest growth of a selection of assets RNZ compared.
A single dollar invested in Bitcoin ten years ago would have grown to be worth between $102 and $103, even though the value slipped recently .
A dollar invested in the S&P500 would have turned into $4.70.
A dollar in the NZX50 would have turned into $2, and $1.20 to $1.30 in interest-reinvested government bonds.
An investment in the Auckland property market was bottom of the table of returns compared. A dollar invested ten years ago would be worth $1.09 now.

But Rupert Carlyon, founder of Koura, which runs a bitcoin KiwiSaver fund said while Bitcoin had delivered the strongest returns, it was also very risky. It would have been unwise for anyone to put all their money into the cryptocurrency ten years ago.

He said of the investments included, he would only be willing to "bet the house" on the S&P500 being worth more in 20 years than it was worth now. He said he was happy with an allocation to Bitcoin in his portfolio but would not put the whole thing into it.

Otago University economist Murat Ungor agreed that the decade-long figure hid significant volatility, "including drawdowns of 70 percent to 80 percent along the way, and the result is highly sensitive to the start and end dates".
An investment in the Auckland property market was bottom of the table of returns compared - but the figures may not tell the entire story.

He said the true return on Auckland housing was being understated because an investor would have also received rental income over the decade, but would also have had to pay rates, maintenance and mortgage interest.

"There are a few important points or caveats to keep in mind. Because New Zealand prices rose substantially over the decade, housing and bond returns likely lost purchasing power in real terms. Additionally, the S&P 500 return is affected by NZD/USD exchange rate fluctuations."
Generate investment specialist Greg Smith said Bitcoin was a good example of why diversification mattered.

"Even after those extraordinary long-term gains, it's down around 30 percent this year and has experienced some enormous swings along the way. I'd be very surprised if the table looked the same in another ten years. Leadership changes between asset classes, and we simply don't know today what will be sitting at the top in 2036.

"Equities are interesting in that regard. When you look historically at decade-long periods rather than individual years, returns tend to become more consistent as the ups and downs of individual years are smoothed out. That doesn't remove risk, but time and diversification have historically been powerful allies for investors. That's really the case for diversification. You don't need to correctly pick the winner of the next decade. You want exposure to a range of assets so you can participate wherever those returns come from."
University of Queensland senior finance lecturer Gertjan Verdickt said cryptocurrencies were a FOMO investment.
"If we disentangle why crypto moves over time, it either has to come from rational reasons or from more behavioural reasons. We do find that actual fundamentals do not drive the price.
"What is a predictor is price - lower priced crypto outperforms higher price cryptos, which aligns with a speculative motive.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/regional/2798: After weeks of controversial headlines and hours of public submissions, Wellington's mayor is still holding back from stating his position on the capital's major rating debate.
Andrew Little said he's forming a "very clear picture" of his view on the ratings system proposal, but didn't want to get ahead of the process with final submissions underway.

The council received about 5700 public submissions and over 450 requests to speak on the city's rating review - which also includes proposals to decrease businesses rates.

In an interview with RNZ, Little was asked what his view was on the controversial policy. He said he did not want to pre-empt the process.

"The whole issue of pre-determination does loom large in local government, so we are sensitive to it, particularly on big and controversial questions like this, so it is important we don't look like we've made up our minds before we've made a decision - otherwise people get cynical about the whole consultation process."

Little, however, said feedback from the community , and information received in the consultation process, would "weigh heavily" on the council's decision over its rating system, and suggested it would feature in his.

"I was neutral from the outset, although I'd met with people who were kind of, championing the cause, they could never explain to me what the impact would be, and until I was clear about that I didn't have a view one way or the other, but now I've got some good information to make a decision."

"There wouldn't be a councillor who hasn't had a donation from somebody who represents one view or another."
When asked whether the presence of these groups had influenced councillors, Little said he wasn't concerned.

"I'm not fazed by lobby groups, interest groups, pressure groups - whatever. It actually enriches our public debate. I think the job of those in elected public office is to use those discriminatory tools and understand that things said with the greatest passion or volume aren't necessarily correct."
Independent councillor for the Pukehīnau Lambton ward, Nicola Young, said the ratings debate was "boiling over" in the city.
"I've been a councillor for 13 years, and never have I experienced the level of public concern that I have about this.

"I went to the orchestra, people came to me beforehand, during the interval and as I was going home. I'm getting emails all the time, people will stop me in the street - people are worried sick about it."
Hours of back-to-back public hearings held in council offices this week have canvassed a range of views on the different proposals.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/environment/2: An invasive cane toad "the size of a guinea pig" was spotted in Tauranga this week.
Volunteer firefighter Annie Henley was training by the Tauranga Model Powerboat Club in Tauriko on Tuesday night when she saw the poisonous toad.

Resources Minister Shane Jones has promised to pause and review the $200 million Gas Security Fund after officials said it was a fossil fuel industry subsidy.
Jones labelled that a "heretical conclusion" but said if he's returned to government he would look into it further to better understand the implications for international trade agreements.
The fund aims to bring gas to market more quickly and can support things like drilling in existing fields, exploration and storage.
Jones and other ministers have repeatedly denied it provided subsidies, and the Greens - who have long criticised the fund - are now accusing them of lying.

In September the government revealed the first investment: $23.5 million in loans for two projects run by Todd Energy which were expected to boost the country's gas reserves with enough to power 80,000 households annually.
The Greens circulated official documents - originally released to the New Zealand Herald - which showed foreign affairs staff advised the investments were "likely to be considered subsidies".
Officials drafted talking points (some of which are redacted) saying when the fund was established, investments were not expected to be subsidies.
"However, it has become clear that, in some cases, time-limited and targeted subsidies are needed to support energy security."
There were strong policy grounds for the investment, they said, pointing to the need to maintain reliable electricity supply during the transition to renewables.
Offering fossil fuel subsidies could breach the terms of some international trade deals, however officials noted the loans were consistent with such agreements.
In separate documents, Treasury officials warned the loans to Todd Energy were comparatively concessionary - that is, at a better rate than the commercial market would offer.
"We could have invested equity into various options to boost oil and gas, but we entered into financial arrangements where the money has to be paid back," he said.

Jones said officials had offered "narrow, globalist-driven interpretations", while the government wanted to accelerate the delivery of oil and gas to "rescue the economy", particularly while New Zealanders faced energy hardship.
"We are entitled to enter into arrangements with financial instruments that are loans," he said.
"We're not obliged to accept every word from Treasury, and it'll be a long day in hell before I ever accept every word from MFAT."
However given the potential trade implications, Jones said he would take a closer look if he was to govern again.
"It wouldn't be unreasonable for us to pause and and better understand why these heretical conclusions have been reached by MFAT and Treasury."
Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the government had repeatedly made false claims about the fund by denying it was a subsidy.
"Ministers had once insisted these subsidies weren't subsidies because the Crown would be investing on commercial terms.
"But, in black and white, taxpayers are now lending Todd Energy 70 per cent of the cost of drilling these wells on terms cheaper than commercial lending."
In response, Jones said the Green Party was deeply hostile to the fossil fuel sector.
The fund is designed to tackle swiftly dwindling gas supplies.
Government information about the two Todd projects said they expected to have gas flowing by the end of next year, using its existing fields and infrastructure.
The fund could also be used for new explorations, though official advice showed no new gas fields were likely to be discovered and developed before 2035 .
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/health/280087: There has been an outbreak of gastroenteritis (gastro) linked to a school camp in the Waikato, attended by more than 400 people.

About 360 students, 13 staff and 48 parents attended the camp.

Medical officer of health Kate Meerkerk said some people who didn't go to the camp but who live with someone who did have also been sick "which shows that gastro can spread from person to person at home".
Meerkerk said the cause wasn't yet known and the National Public Health Service was investigating and working to confirm how many people were affected.

"Public Health staff are working closely with the school and the camp to understand what may have caused it, including potentially food, water or the wider environment. Stool sample kits have been provided to the school, and we are asking people with recent vomiting or diarrhoea to help by providing a sample as soon as possible so we can find the cause."
People with gastro should stay away from school until they have had no symptoms for 48 hours.

"Most people with gastro recover at home within a few days without needing medical treatment. If you are concerned, call your usual health care provider or Healthline on 0800 611 116, any time, for free. For more information visit info.health.nz ."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/crime-and-jus: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/crime-and-justice/2775509%2Ffrench-tourist-maelle-favregros-fatal-fall-in-popular-alpine-area-prompts-safety-warnings
Social media is leading some tourists to take risks and venture into the outdoors unprepared , a coroner says.

French tourist Maëlle Favregros died from blood loss after falling while crossing slippery, rocky terrain near the Brewster Glacier in Mount Aspiring National Park in February last year, findings released on Thursday said.
The 23-year-old was not wearing tramping boots or on a managed track and had discovered the Brewster Glacier trip on AllTrails.

Coroner Alexandra Cunninghame urged trampers to plan their routes using official sources - including the Department of Conservation (DOC) and Plan My Walk - be aware of hazards, stay on official marked routes and have the necessary skills and gear for alpine trips.
There were seven search and rescues in the area last year, six in 2024, seven in 2023, as well as another death in 2020.
Mountain Safety Council chief executive Mike Daisley said the coroner's findings aimed to stop such tragedies from repeating.

"Maëlle's death occurred in terrain beyond the managed DOC track network in an alpine environment where significant natural hazards exist and where visitor judgement, preparation and decision-making are critical factors in maintaining safety," he said.
The Brewster Glacier area was reasonably quiet and not many people explored it until about six years ago when suddenly there was a spike in visits and a lot of interest, Daisley said.
Trampers should use social media for ideas but not for preparation, he said.

"Social media in itself is not the problem. Use that for inspiration, but don't consider that your plan. Do some investigating and find out about the environment that you've decided just because you've seen a picture of it, and it's great to be inspired by it, but do your research."
The Brewster Glacier is accessed via the steep Brewster Track which climbs about 1000 metres over about 2.8 kilometres.
An interagency group had been set up in April 2024 to help raise awareness of the hazards in the area after a rise in people getting into trouble.
It prompted a new Brewster Track safety video to be released last November highlighting the hazards.
The Department of Conservation carried out a review of Favregros' death and had made several changes to boost awareness of the hazards.

They included installing new signs at the carpark and at Brewster Hut warning of the risks, targeted social media advertising about safety and planning for the track, and working with AllTrails so people were aware of the hazards, risks and skills needed.

"The increasing use has been mirrored by an increase in visitor incidents requiring search and rescue involvement, mainly associated with visitors getting into difficulty when attempting to access areas off the DOC managed experience, such as Mt Armstrong and the Brewster Glacier," the review said.
The Department of Conservation's Central Otago operations manager, Charlie Sklenar, said beautiful pictures online were not showing the risks involved at the locations they drew people towards.

"Social media's inspiring people to visit some incredible places [but] our concern is people heading into challenging terrain without understanding what's required. We want people to be inspired by social media but we also don't want them to rely on that alone to plan their trips," Sklenar said.
She said the department had created its own social media messaging to direct tourists towards reliable information about the areas they were visiting.

It's been a night of reflection and waiata on Manderson Grove for a crowd of Lower Hutt locals protesting the sale of public housing.
Almost the entire street is on the market, pitched as an opportunity for developers, investors and landbankers , with a deadline sale of 8 December.
Kāinga Ora said it was selling properties that are costly to maintain, and that the units on Manderson Grove are old and no longer fit for purpose.
A spokesperson said the proceeds from the sale would be reinvested in social housing in the region, and selling the land provided the opportunity for new housing to be developed.
But some in the community say public land should stay in public ownership. On Wednesday night they took their protest to the site, camping out overnight among the empty houses on Manderson Grove.
Jade Hakaraia, a member of St David's Anglican Church, was one of those who took up the vigil overnight.

"I think it was 2 o'clock in the morning [on Thursday], and I just felt this prompting to walk around and look into the houses and I was imagining the cars in the carport, families walking into their homes through the gates, children on the street."
She said she understood the stability and community that state housing provided.
"With the housing going elsewhere, it's like they have to rebuild that from the beginning. And that's really hard for anyone."
Former Manderson Grove resident George Wi Edward Crown said being told he and his grandkids would have to leave was "shattering".
"I was born and brought up in number 11 Manderson Grove from about five years old.
"My mum lived here. When my dad passed away in 1990, I moved back with my kids and my family to look after my mum. She just recently passed away in 2023. So she was here for 47 years."
"Oh, it's emotional. When you get taken out of a place you're brought up in all your life, it's not nice. It feels like your heart's been ripped out."
Crown said the community he'd known for decades had been broken up and dispersed.
Former Manderson Grove resident George Wi Edward Crown said being told to leave was "shattering".
Kāinga Ora said the agency had considered redeveloping the site but said "it did not represent good value for money compared with other opportunities to invest in social housing".
Protester and development manager with the Wellington Anglican Diocese, Nick Young, said the sections were prime real estate and he felt it made sense to continue the history of public housing.
"It's a fantastic bit of flat land in a beautiful little cul-de-sac grove in the middle of the Hutt Valley. What's not to like about this?" he said.
The land was likely to be among the easiest to develop pieces of land in the area, he said.
"If there's a need here ... why wouldn't you want to respond to that need by developing in this space?"
As of September 2026, 339 households were on the public housing waitlist in Lower Hutt.
Kāinga Ora said it owned 3700 homes in Lower Hutt and, in the past three years, it had increased its housing stock by 255.

Road safety advocates are calling for more driving licence testing options as wait times at VTNZ stretched past 80 days at some sites.
Driving Change Network said New Zealanders trying to get their licence before Summer were stuck in long queues for a test.
It said it was the second time in three years that a "poorly timed policy change" had pushed wait times out.
National director of the network, Wendy Robertson, told Checkpoint the graduated driver licensing changes on 25 January were causing the rush.
"Three pressures are landing at the same time," Robertson said.
"Learners who already qualify to sit their restricted test are trying to book before the changes add another six months to their time.

"Restricted drivers who have picked up police driving infringements since May are trying to sit their full test before an extra six-month penalty applies. And on top of that comes the usual December rush, when young people finish exams and get ready for holiday jobs, summer travel and moving to uni."
Robertson said VTNZ would have known demand was going to be higher at this time of year.
"Letting staffing drop so it can't keep up is really not good enough."

Figures extracted from NZTA's Driver Licence Register showed North and West Auckland wait times were more than 42 days for a restricted test and 36 days for a full test, while in South Auckland it was more than 50 days for a restricted test and more than 37 for a full test, the network said.
In Canterbury it was more than 46 days for a restricted test and 38 for a full test.
Some individual sites were under severe pressure - Auckland's New Lynn was more than 62 days for a practical test, Auckland's Wiri was more than 82 and Nelson was more than 60.
"We understand demand will drop from late January when the full licence test is removed, and we can see why VTNZ may not have replaced staff who resigned," Robertson said.
"But VTNZ is contracted by the government to deliver this service, and it should still be able to deliver it."
Robertson said NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi (NZTA) was helping by pressing VTNZ to add testing days and hours.
"This shows exactly why New Zealand needs two testing options, not the monopoly VTNZ has held since 2014."
Under the new system, learners could shorten the restricted period back to six months, with more supervised driving or paying for an approved course.
NZTA's head of driving regulation, Chris Rodley, said NZTA was working with VTNZ and the network to create more testing capacity in Canterbury.

At least 200 extra testing days would be introduced in the next eight weeks in the region, he said, through travelling driver testing officers, while recruitment and training of additional officers was completed.

"We are also working to reduce missed appointments through targeted engagement and nationwide text reminders sent 24 hours before practical tests, and we are encouraging people to consider alternative locations near their preferred test sites, as wait times can vary and it might be worth travelling further for an earlier test time."

Wednesday marked the deadline for schools to express their interest in offering an additional exam session, after students faced login problems and lost work during online exams on 12 November.

"We know students have worked hard this year to prepare for their exams. This additional exam opportunity gives students another chance to demonstrate their knowledge and skills," Marshall said.

"Students eligible for Special Assessment Conditions will be able to receive that support if their school is aware they intend to sit the exam," Marshall said.

The New Plymouth District Council has decided to push ahead with an $8.9 million upgrade of the city's zoo - despite its aim of saving $20 million as part of its long-term plan process.
Nestled in the wider Pukekura Park area, Brooklands Zoo attracts about 140,000 visitors a year and is popular destination for families with young children.
It features otter and meerkat enclosures, an aviary, primate areas as well as farm animals.

Councillors had to decide to approve a draft strategic vision for the zoo's future and push ahead with exhibit upgrades - which had been years in the planning - or pause the project and reconsider its funding as part of the 2027-2037 long-term plan.
The zoo costs about $870,000 annually to run and a council officers report warned its enclosures were showing signs of wear and tear and approaching end of life.
Following the upgrade it would have about a third less exhibits - 29 species to 21 - fewer individual animals and roughly eight fewer habitats.
Capybaras recently exhibited at the zoo had already been relocated, the report said.
A otter enclosure would cost about $1.7m, a new aviary $3.1m while new primate areas $3.6m.
Councillor John Woodward moved that the project got put on hold.
"Absolutely support the zoo, but this is based on the previous council's decisions and the previous council's LTP.

"For me this is still spending ratepayer money that we should given the current climate bring into our LTP coming. For me this is about doing the right thing, doing our due diligence, looking at the books, so we own it, we inherit it and we move on."
Veteran councillor Gordon Brown - who in 2024 decried the then $1.5m budget to upgrade the otters' enclosure, it's now $1.7m - agreed.
"It's too much $8.9 million. It's a regional zoo that brings in no revenue whatsoever. It's got a lovely enclosed playground that's safe for families and we throw them the free bonus of a zoo.
"I felt the budget was way over the top and we should've chucked it back and reconfigured the project in keeping with what we could afford and what was needed."
Brown was particularly incensed the zoo and managed to generate external revenue of only $900 over an entire year.
Woodward's motion was lost 6-8 and councillors were left to decided whether to move with the project, continue with alterations or consider laying it on the table.
Councillor David Bublitz moved the motion approving pushing ahead with stage one of the project.

"During deliberations on the 2024 LTP I think more that 60 percent of people that responded were in favour of the council decision or even more money being spent on the zoo to ensure that it got up to standard and remained safe and accessible and compliant with regulations.

"The decision had already been made, the money was already budgeted for this financial year. The mood around the table was that they were all in favour of the zoo anyway, so I just didn't understand why we would delay it for another six, seven or eight months when everyone was going to vote in favour of it effectively in the next long-term plan."
"I took my kids, I went there as a kid myself. Hopefully when my daughters come back to New Plymouth and I've got granddads I'll get to take them as well. It's one of the icons of New Plymouth."
Mayor Max Brough had a bob each way ... voting in favour of the motion to pause the project and when that was lost voting in favour of pushing on.
"I changed my mind through that discussion. I see the value in us having a zoo and it is something that brings people to town and it's one of our features.
https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/friends-p: Two best friends have set a Guinness World Record for the highest-ever game of chess played on a mountain, after climbing all the way to the summit of an Ecuadorian volcano to do it.

Americans Adam Wininger, 32, and Joshua Host, 44, set up their chess board at the top of Chimborazo, a mountain in Ecuador, at a height of 20,593 feet, which is more than 6,200 metres above sea level.
Their climb beat the previous record of 20,393 feet, which was set by two British climbers on a mountain in Nepal back in 2024, by exactly 200 feet.
The pair had actually tried to reach the summit once before, but bad weather forced them to turn back. This time, they made it all the way to the top with their chess set in hand.
“It’s our favourite game and there is something so epic about playing it on top of a mountain,” Wininger told Guinness World Records.
He joked that if anyone ever beats their record, the pair will simply climb even higher to reclaim it, by exactly 200 feet every time.
For now, the chess-loving duo can enjoy their spot in the record books, all the way up in the clouds.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/spacecraf: A European spacecraft has sent back the first close-up pictures of an asteroid that was deliberately smashed into by a NASA spacecraft, as part of a test to protect Earth one day.
The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft arrived at the Didymos-Dimorphos asteroid system this week and released its first detailed images on 25 November 2026.

Dimorphos is a small “moonlet” asteroid that orbits a larger asteroid called Didymos. Back in 2022, NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft called DART into Dimorphos, in the first-ever test of what scientists call “planetary defence.”

The idea is simple: if a dangerous asteroid were ever heading towards Earth, could humans crash something into it to change its path and keep our planet safe? The DART test showed that it can work. The impact changed Dimorphos’s orbit around Didymos by just over 30 minutes.
Now Hera’s job is to study the crater DART left behind, to help scientists understand exactly what happened and how big the effect was.
“ESA’s Hera mission has arrived to learn the answers we need to know,” said mission lead Patrick Michel.
Hera will stay at the asteroid system for months, using cameras and other instruments to learn more about how to keep Earth safe from space rocks in the future.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/giant-new: Northland has its first wind farm, with power company Mercury officially opening the $287 million Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm near Dargaville on Monday.

The wind farm sits at Ōmāmari, on the region’s west coast, on farmland run by Pāmu. Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton cut the ribbon alongside Kaipara Deputy Mayor Gordon Lambeth and Northland MP Grant McCallum.
“Today we recognise the skill and commitment of everyone who has helped bring Northland’s first wind farm to life,” Hamilton said.

The wind farm has 12 huge turbines, each standing 206 metres tall from the ground to the tip of the blade when it’s pointing straight up. That makes them the tallest turbines in New Zealand, and the second-tallest structures in the whole country, beaten only by Auckland’s Sky Tower.
Together, the turbines can make about 77 megawatts of electricity. That’s enough power for more than 31,000 homes once the wind farm is running at full strength.
Construction began in March last year, and Mercury says the project remains on schedule and on budget, with full power generation expected by 2027.
“We remain on track to complete the Kaiwaikawe development on schedule and on budget,” Hamilton said.
Wind farms like this one help New Zealand make electricity without burning fuels like coal or gas, which is better for the environment and for the climate.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/air-nz-br: Air New Zealand is flying long-haul routes from Christchurch again, after a non-stop flight to Singapore took off on 28 October 2026. Long-haul flights are very long trips, often across oceans. Since 2020, the airline had flown very few of them from Christchurch.
More routes are on the way. Direct flights to Tokyo in Japan start on 28 November, and flights to Perth in Australia start on 30 November. A seasonal service to Bali is planned for winter 2027.

Christchurch Airport is expecting its busiest international summer yet, with 21 percent more international seats than before. That’s roughly one extra seat for every five. Even so, Auckland still handles nearly three times as many passengers.

Will smaller towns benefit? Christchurch is also a hub, or meeting point, for flights to smaller places like Queenstown, Dunedin, Nelson, Hokitika and Invercargill. Ajai Jayathilakan, an aviation lecturer at Massey University, warns that these regional communities could miss out.

Figures from NZ Airports looked at routes where another airline, Jetstar, doesn’t compete with Air NZ. On those routes, fares rose 4.2 percent and seat numbers dropped by the same amount. Billie Moore, who led NZ Airports at the time, said, “Regional New Zealand is living the reality of this every day.”
Jayathilakan says the new flights are good news for the South Island. He says ideas like better-linked flight timetables could help smaller towns share in the benefits.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/famous-ba: One of the Batmobiles from the 1992 film Batman Returns is going up for auction near Los Angeles, in the United States. It could become the most expensive Batmobile ever sold.

Julien’s Auctions expects the car to sell for between US$5 million and US$7 million, which is about NZ$9 million to NZ$12 million. The current record is US$4.6 million (about NZ$8.4 million). It was set in 2013 by the Batmobile Adam West drove in the 1960s Batman TV series.
Three special Batmobiles were built for Batman Returns, which was directed by Tim Burton. Julien’s calls this one the “Number One Hero car”, and it was used in most of the film’s driving scenes.
The glossy black car is about six metres long and has two large tail fins. It still has its original paint, a Chevrolet V-8 engine, and a remote-controlled exhaust that shoots out flames.
Julien’s called it “one of the most recognised and important cinematic vehicles in Hollywood history.”
However, the new owner won’t be cruising the streets in it. The car is not street legal, which means it can’t be driven on public roads. It must also stay parked whenever it’s shown to the public.
The car has spent years on display at the Marconi Automotive Museum in California, and the auction takes place in Gardena on Tuesday.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/black-cap: The Black Caps battled through a windy final day at the Basin Reserve in Wellington to draw the first cricket Test against India on 23 November 2026.
India had scored 720 runs for nine wickets before declaring, which means choosing to stop batting. That gave them a huge lead of 352 runs.

To save the match, New Zealand had to bat for the whole day without losing all their wickets. They started at 119 for two and played so carefully that it took 18 balls to score their first run of the morning.

Devon Conway made 65 and Rachin Ravindra made 37 before both were out. Glenn Phillips, who scored a century in the first innings, made 26. He and Daryl Mitchell put on 63 runs together, and Mitchell finished not out on 49.
New Zealand were 239 for five when the captains shook hands to end the match. India were still five wickets short of a win.
In Test cricket, if time runs out before either team can win, the match is a draw.
